The New Sweet Spot for 1440p is now 2070 🤩  It Sits between 1080 & 1080ti in traditional rasterization.  

2070 has Less Cuda Cores & texture units than the 1080( 2304 vs 2560 & 144TU vs 160TU)  yet the 2070 is  faster -till now the gap will increases as drivers will become more optimized , developers get use to the new architecture etc.

2070 (TU 106) :445mm2 , 10.8 billion transistors 

1080(GP 104): 314 mm² , 7.2 billion transistors

With an added advantage of : 

DLSS ( 25 Supported titles till now waiting to be patched only including PUBG , Shadow of the Tomraider , FF 15 ...)   , RT Cores , Tensor Cores , AI , Neural Networks 

HDR Tone Mapping 

Hybrid Rendering 

Dedicated HDR PipeLine to reduce latency with HDR , HDR on Pascal is a real latency mess up since it is SW processed.

GDDR6 (448 GB/s vs 320 GB/s of memory bandwidth on the 1080)

DP 1.4 with DSC 

RT 

It is a definite leap in technology.

HardOCP: 

Is Turing Faster?

With both video cards operating nearly at the same frequency this creates an interesting scenario. We are basically looking at two video cards with similar clock speeds. We can estimate if GeForce RTX 2070’s Turing architecture might be faster than the previous Pascal architecture. It is important to realize there are more SM Units but less CUDA Cores (64 CUDA cores per SM versus 128 on Pascal) and Texture Units on GeForce RTX 2070 when compared to GeForce GTX 1080. In terms of GPU performance, this would mean slower performance on GeForce RTX 2070 if clock speed is the same. However, Turing is a new architecture. There are technically more SM Units, even if there are less CUDA Cores per SM. What we can then gather is if the architectural changes make up for the loss in overall CUDA Cores and Texture Units.
According to our testing the results all signs point to yes, the Turing architecture is definitely superior to, and faster than, the Pascal architecture at similar clock speeds. In all of our testing the MSI GeForce RTX 2070 GAMING Z consistently provided faster performance at 1440p and 4K compared to the MSI GeForce GTX 1080 GAMING X video card, despite having a CUDA Core and Texture Unit deficit, at the same clock speeds. text:
GTX1080 makes no sense if about the same price as an RTX2070... again RTX even if never used also doesn't add to the price. So here's the main advantages as I see it:
1) DLSS profiles in some games (up to maybe 40% higher FPS... Digital Foundry also showed the AA was better than most other methods)

2) RTRT (may not be practical but then again as they optimize the code maybe it will be. Certainly a 2.5D game like Diablo 3 which isn't too demanding could be run at a high res, 60FPS and still have lots of ray-tracing added like light-based magic, shadows in general etc)

3) drivers (as said more of a long-term thing where driver support drops off. not a big deal really IMO)

4) non-gaming applications: newer CUDA using INT32 and other apps using Tensor cores etc could do amazing things in theory.

5) *DSC: Display Stream Compression
This last one is actually very important. There's a recent 4K/144Hz monitor that drops quality down to (4:2:2?) or drops refresh to 98Hz at 4:4:4 due to insufficient bandwidth. If the monitor has DSC (not certain if it does) and the card does which apparently Turing does then you can get up to 4K@244Hz at 4:4:4.

6) Other: improved decode/encode (can for example decode HEVC 4K 4:4:4 12)... probably other minor stuff too.

7) VR USB Type C (I think that's new. could be wrong)... handles everything to the VR headset with one cable.

8) HDR hardware (more efficient but also means benchmarks comparing HDR games to previous GTX cards can be misleading as it takes a big more 
processing to do HDR on previous. I think it's around 5% FPS hit but not certain. I don't think AMD VEGA is affected as it seems to have hardware support like the new Turing cards).

text:
This so much. People keep talking shit on ray-tracing, but ray-tracing is an industry standard in film and special effects. And for good reason. It both looks worlds better, and is also actually easier to implement in a scene. 
Right now artists have to fake light to convince the player that it is correct. This takes time to fine tune, and even then sometimes falls flat and ruins the illusion. Ray-tracing takes out the guess work and fine tuning, and just does it for the artist. Studios don't just want to switch to ray-tracing just because it will look better, but because it will be easier on the studio's budget. 
Ray-tracing will eventually be the standard of games. I promise this. The question is if it will be via RTX, or some other method.

text: Aerospace engineer here, and I have to nitpick that fan. The EVGA "G" logos on the fan blades looks like they stick out physically? These can cause pretty bad flow separation at high speeds and pretty much drop flow pressure by a significant amount. Clearly this isn't the case in your thermals, but still, it could have been something; and probably marketing added them last minute before engineering could chip in (does EVGA do CFD on their fans? Noctua does for example). Adding bumps to blades (airfoils) can actually improve flow since it encourages the turbulent boundary layer to stay stuck to the surface longer (delays flow separation), but these need to be in a pattern and placed in the right places (for example, Noctua has raised strips on their blades). The G logo definitely doesn't fit this bill; they got lucky in a sense that they don't cause issues with flow at high RPM.

@Nik Senior There are two problems with your analysis. First you list BFV as having achieved 152 fps, but that is only true under DX11. Ray tracing is an extension to DX12, not DX11. Under DX12 BFV only achieved 136 fps.

Given this, the 1440p is all but ruled out for ray tracing. The 2080 ti should get you ~25% boost in performance, but you'd lose more than that just pushing 1440p pixels. And of course, at 1440p the ray tracing pass would also take significantly longer, leaving even less time to render the base image.

Second you are applying ray tracing timings from a purpose built closed room demo to the varied open levels of a real running game. There is no reason to believe the 9.2ms needed to implement ray tracing in the demo would be the same for Battlefield V. In fact it should take longer.

We simply will have no idea how long ray tracing will take in BFV until someone can actually benchmark ray tracing in BFV. That is why no reviewer is vouching for the ray tracing claims of the RTX cards.
